IN-1.t: Identify the epidermal layers from stratum basale to stratum corneum and describe how keratinocytes change in each (keratins 5 and 14 to 1 and 10, keratohyalin granules, lamellar bodies, loss of nuclei), noting that stratum lucidum appears only in thick skin.

Identify melanocytes (neural crest origin, melanin transfer to keratinocytes), Langerhans cells (bone marrow origin, Birbeck granules, CD1a, antigen presentation), and Merkel cells (basal layer touch receptors) by epidermal location and function.

Compare desmosomes (desmogleins), hemidesmosomes (BP180 or collagen XVII, BP230, integrin alpha6 beta4), and adherens junctions (E-cadherin), and predict the blistering disease that results when desmosomal or hemidesmosomal proteins are targeted by autoantibodies or mutation.

Describe the dermal-epidermal junction (lamina lucida with laminin 332 and collagen XVII anchoring filaments, lamina densa with type IV collagen, type VII collagen anchoring fibrils) and predict the level of the split when each component fails.

Compare the papillary dermis, reticular dermis, and hypodermis by connective tissue density, vessels, and sensory receptors (Meissner corpuscles in dermal papillae, Pacinian corpuscles in deep dermis and subcutis, free nerve endings).

Distinguish eccrine, apocrine, and sebaceous glands by location, secretion, and control (eccrine glands by sympathetic cholinergic fibers, apocrine glands opening into axillary and anogenital hair follicles, sebaceous glands holocrine and androgen driven), and relate hyperhidrosis to eccrine glands and acne to sebaceous glands.
IN-1.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: sweat and sebaceous glands: hyperhidrosis

IN-1.t: Describe the hair follicle (bulb, dermal papilla, bulge stem cells, arrector pili) and nail unit (matrix, plate, bed, folds), and relate anagen, catagen, and telogen to telogen effluvium and the lateral nail fold to an ingrown nail.
IN-1.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: hair and hair follicles; nails

IN-1.t: Define acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, spongiosis, acantholysis, and dyskeratosis, and match each to an example disease such as psoriasis, eczema, or pemphigus.

IN-2.t: Distinguish derivatives of surface ectoderm (epidermis, hair, nails, cutaneous and mammary glands, lens, anterior pituitary, tooth enamel) from those of neuroectoderm (central nervous system, retina, posterior pituitary) and neural crest.

Identify neural crest derivatives relevant to skin and nerves (melanocytes, Schwann cells, dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, odontoblasts), and explain why facial dermis arises from neural crest while dermis of the back arises from somite dermatomes.

Describe fetal skin development, including the periderm, epidermal stratification, melanoblast migration from the neural crest, hair bud and dermal papilla formation, lanugo, and vernix caseosa as a protective coat of sebum and shed cells.

Explain why melanocytes arrested in the dermis during migration produce dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots), and distinguish it from congenital melanocytic nevi, infantile hemangiomas, and port-wine stains in newborns.
IN-2.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Congenital disorders: benign lesions in neonates, infants, and children

IN-2.t: Explain why failed melanoblast migration in piebaldism produces congenital white patches lacking melanocytes, whereas albinism shows normal melanocyte numbers with reduced melanin synthesis.

IN-3.t: Describe the plasma membrane components (phospholipid bilayer, cholesterol, integral and peripheral proteins, glycocalyx) and explain how cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity and how unsaturated fatty acids increase it.

Compare simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, primary active transport, secondary active transport, and endocytosis by energy source, saturability, and direction, using the Na+/K+-ATPase, GLUT transporters, and SGLT1 as examples.
Predict how inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) changes intracellular sodium, cell volume, and membrane potential, and relate this to cellular swelling in hypoxic cell injury.
Explain osmosis, distinguish osmolarity from tonicity, and predict cell volume in isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic solutions, including why urea is an ineffective osmole.

Calculate an ion's equilibrium potential with the Nernst equation, and explain how potassium leak channels, the Goldman equation, and the Gibbs-Donnan effect of impermeant intracellular anions establish the resting membrane potential.

Predict how hyperkalemia depolarizes and hypokalemia hyperpolarizes the resting membrane potential, and explain why sustained depolarization inactivates voltage-gated sodium channels and lowers nerve and muscle excitability.
IN-3.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance disorders: hypokalemia, hyperkalemia

IN-3.t: Explain how CFTR mutation blocks chloride reabsorption in the eccrine sweat duct, raising sweat chloride to 60 mmol/L or higher, while it blocks chloride secretion in airway epithelium.
IN-3.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: cystic fibrosis

IN-4.t: Explain how the hypothalamus integrates core and skin thermoreceptor input around a set point, with the anterior (preoptic) hypothalamus driving heat loss and the posterior hypothalamus driving heat conservation and production.

Compare heat loss by radiation, conduction, convection, and evaporation, and predict why sweat evaporation becomes the only route when ambient temperature exceeds skin temperature and why high humidity impairs cooling.

Explain heat conservation and production by cutaneous vasoconstriction, piloerection, shivering, thyroid hormone, and nonshivering thermogenesis through UCP1 (thermogenin) in brown fat, and why neonates depend on brown fat.
Explain how IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha induce hypothalamic PGE2 to raise the set point in fever, and distinguish fever from hyperthermia, in which the set point is unchanged.
IN-4.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Toxins and environmental extremes: temperature (hyperthermia)

IN-4.t: Distinguish heat exhaustion from heat stroke (core temperature above 40 °C (104 °F) with central nervous system dysfunction), compare classic and exertional heat stroke, and predict rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and DIC.
IN-4.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Toxins and environmental extremes: temperature (hyperthermia, heat stroke)

IN-4.t: Explain how an RYR1 mutation causes malignant hyperthermia after volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine through uncontrolled sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release, producing muscle rigidity, hypercarbia, and rising core temperature.
IN-4.usmle: Musculoskeletal System: Adverse effects of drugs: malignant hyperthermia

IN-4.t: Describe hypothermia (core below 35 °C (95 °F)), including loss of shivering when severe, bradycardia, Osborn (J) waves, and arrhythmias, and distinguish frostbite (ice crystals, endothelial injury, thrombosis) from perniosis (nonfreezing damp cold).
IN-4.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Toxins and environmental extremes: temperature (hypothermia); Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: frostbite, perniosis

IN-5.t: Trace collagen synthesis (prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation needing vitamin C and Fe2+, glycosylation, triple helix formation, procollagen peptidase cleavage, lysyl oxidase cross-linking needing copper) and predict the connective tissue defect when each step fails.
IN-5.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: structural protein disorders

IN-5.t: Relate vitamin C deficiency to scurvy findings (perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, bleeding gums, poor wound healing) and defective copper transport in Menkes disease to brittle kinky hair and connective tissue weakness.
IN-5.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Nutrition: vitamin C

IN-5.t: Explain the photosensitive dermatitis of niacin deficiency (pellagra) and its causes, including corn-based diets, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome, and isoniazid-induced vitamin B6 deficiency.
IN-5.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Nutrition: vitamin B3 (niacin)

IN-5.t: Distinguish skin findings of deficiency of vitamin A (follicular hyperkeratosis, xerosis), zinc (acrodermatitis enteropathica with periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, poor healing), biotin (dermatitis, alopecia), riboflavin (angular cheilitis), and essential fatty acids (scaly dermatitis).
IN-5.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Nutrition: vitamin A; mineral deficiencies

IN-5.t: Trace vitamin D synthesis from 7-dehydrocholesterol in the epidermis by UVB to cholecalciferol, then 25-hydroxylation in the liver and 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney, and predict how dark skin, high latitude, and sunscreen reduce it.
IN-5.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Nutrition: vitamin D

IN-5.t: Describe the stratum corneum lipid barrier (ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids from lamellar bodies), sebum composition (triglycerides, wax esters, squalene), and dermal glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronic acid and dermatan sulfate.

Relate xanthoma type to lipid disorder: eruptive xanthomas with severe hypertriglyceridemia (lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency), tendon xanthomas and xanthelasma with familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor), and palmar xanthomas with dysbetalipoproteinemia (apoE2).
IN-5.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: benign: xanthomas

IN-5.t: Explain how uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency in porphyria cutanea tarda causes blistering, fragility, and hypertrichosis on sun-exposed skin, and identify triggers such as alcohol, hepatitis C, iron overload, and estrogen.
IN-5.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: enzymatic/metabolic: porphyria

IN-6.t: Describe how superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radical form (mitochondrial electron leak, NADPH oxidase, UV and ionizing radiation, Fenton reaction with Fe2+) and how they damage membrane lipids, proteins, and DNA.

Explain how superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn cytosolic, Mn mitochondrial), catalase, and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase detoxify reactive oxygen species, and why glutathione regeneration needs NADPH from G6PD in the pentose phosphate pathway.

Explain how non-vitamin antioxidants protect skin, including reduced glutathione, ubiquinol (coenzyme Q10), dietary carotenoids such as lycopene, and melanin, and why eumelanin is more photoprotective than pheomelanin.

Compare UVB injury (direct DNA damage forming cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, sunburn) with UVA injury (deeper penetration, oxidative DNA damage), and explain photoaging through matrix metalloproteinase breakdown of collagen and solar elastosis.
IN-6.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: effects of ultraviolet light

IN-6.t: Explain how the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst and myeloperoxidase kill microbes, and predict recurrent skin abscesses and granulomas with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus in chronic granulomatous disease.
IN-6.usmle: Immune System: Disorders associated with immunodeficiency: phagocyte and NK cell deficiencies: chronic granulomatous disease

IN-7.t: Explain how cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases, Rb, and p53 control the G1 to S checkpoint, and how UV-signature C to T mutations in TP53 drive actinic keratosis and squamous cell carcinoma.
IN-7.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: malignant: squamous cell carcinoma

IN-7.t: Explain how defective nucleotide excision repair in xeroderma pigmentosum (autosomal recessive) causes extreme photosensitivity, early freckling, and basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma in childhood.
IN-7.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Congenital disorders: xeroderma pigmentosum

IN-7.t: Relate driver mutations to skin tumors: PTCH1 loss activating hedgehog signaling in basal cell carcinoma and Gorlin syndrome, BRAF V600E or NRAS in nevi and melanoma, and germline CDKN2A (p16) in familial melanoma.
IN-7.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Neoplasms and related disorders: inherited cancer syndromes

IN-7.t: Interpret pedigrees of skin disorders with autosomal dominant (NF1, tuberous sclerosis, epidermolysis bullosa simplex), autosomal recessive (oculocutaneous albinism, xeroderma pigmentosum), and X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis) inheritance, and calculate recurrence risk for offspring.

Explain the gene products in NF1 (neurofibromin, a Ras GTPase-activating protein on chromosome 17) and tuberous sclerosis (hamartin and tuberin, which inhibit mTOR), and identify café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, ash-leaf macules, and facial angiofibromas.
IN-7.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis

IN-7.t: Explain how loss-of-function filaggrin (FLG) mutations impair the epidermal barrier in ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis, and how steroid sulfatase deficiency causes X-linked ichthyosis in males.
IN-7.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: sweat and sebaceous glands: ichthyosis

IN-7.t: Explain how MSH binding the MC1R receptor raises cAMP and MITF-driven tyrosinase expression to favor eumelanin, and why MC1R loss-of-function variants cause red hair, fair skin, and higher melanoma risk.

IN-8.t: Distinguish hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, and metaplasia by mechanism and example (epidermal hyperplasia in a callus, squamous metaplasia of bronchi in smokers, columnar metaplasia in Barrett esophagus), and explain how metaplasia and pathologic hyperplasia can progress to dysplasia.

Explain how ATP depletion, mitochondrial damage, calcium influx, oxidative stress, and membrane damage injure cells, and distinguish reversible changes (swelling, fatty change, blebbing, ribosome detachment) from irreversible ones (membrane rupture, mitochondrial densities, pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis).

Classify necrosis as coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid, or gangrenous, and predict the type from its setting (myocardial infarct, brain infarct or abscess, tuberculosis, acute pancreatitis, vasculitis, limb ischemia).

Compare intrinsic (BCL-2 family, cytochrome c, caspase-9) and extrinsic (Fas ligand, TNF, caspase-8) apoptosis and perforin-granzyme killing by cytotoxic T cells, and distinguish apoptosis (shrinkage, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation) from necrosis.

Distinguish endogenous pigments (lipofuscin from lipid peroxidation, hemosiderin staining with Prussian blue, melanin, bilirubin) from exogenous pigments (inhaled carbon in anthracosis, tattoo ink held in dermal macrophages), and relate each to its source.
IN-8.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: tattoo

IN-8.t: Distinguish dystrophic calcification (necrotic tissue, normal serum calcium) from metastatic calcification (hypercalcemia, normal tissues), and identify infiltrates of fat (steatosis), cholesterol (foam cells, xanthomas), and amyloid (Congo red with apple-green birefringence).

Distinguish benign from malignant neoplasms by differentiation, anaplasia (pleomorphism, high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, atypical mitoses), invasion, and metastasis, apply tumor naming rules, and distinguish dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, grade, and stage.
IN-8.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Neoplasms and related disorders

IN-8.t: Explain the hallmarks of cancer, including oncogene growth signaling (BRAF in melanoma), two-hit loss of tumor suppressors (RB, TP53), evasion of apoptosis, telomerase activity, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, invasion, Warburg metabolism, and immune evasion.
IN-8.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Neoplasms and related disorders

IN-9.t: Identify normal skin flora (Staphylococcus epidermidis, Cutibacterium acnes, Corynebacterium, Malassezia, nasal Staphylococcus aureus carriage) and explain how flora, acidic pH, sebum fatty acids, desquamation, and antimicrobial peptides resist pathogen colonization.

Trace the stages of a skin infection (entry through a breach, adherence, colonization, invasion, spread, tissue damage) and relate the depth reached to impetigo, folliculitis, erysipelas, cellulitis, abscess, and necrotizing fasciitis.
IN-9.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial

IN-9.t: Distinguish skin disease from direct invasion versus toxins, explaining how exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein 1 in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and how superantigens (TSST-1, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins) cause diffuse rash and shock.
IN-9.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome

IN-9.t: Explain how diabetes, venous insufficiency, lymphedema, tinea pedis fissures, injection drug use, neutropenia, and T cell deficiency predispose to skin infection, and predict the likely organism from the host context.

IN-10.t: Sequence wound healing: hemostasis, inflammation (neutrophils, then macrophages by day 3), proliferation (granulation tissue, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, type III collagen), and remodeling (type I collagen, zinc-dependent metalloproteinases), noting scars regain only about 70 to 80 percent of normal strength.
IN-10.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: burns or wounds affecting skin or subcutaneous tissue

IN-10.t: Compare healing by primary and secondary intention (more granulation tissue, myofibroblast contraction), and explain how infection, diabetes, ischemia, glucocorticoids, malnutrition, vitamin C or zinc deficiency, and foreign bodies delay healing.

Distinguish hypertrophic scars (parallel type III collagen, confined to the wound, may regress) from keloids (disorganized type I and III collagen beyond wound borders, earlobes, darker skin), and identify exuberant granulation tissue, dehiscence, and contracture.
IN-10.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: keloids

IN-10.t: Classify burns as superficial, superficial partial-thickness, deep partial-thickness, or full-thickness by blisters, blanching, and sensation, estimate burned area by the rule of nines, and predict hypovolemia, Pseudomonas sepsis, hypermetabolism, inhalation injury, and contracture.
IN-10.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: burns; thermal injury; Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Toxins and environmental extremes: thermal injury, burns

IN-10.t: Explain why electrical injury causes small entry and exit skin wounds with extensive deep muscle and nerve necrosis, rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuric kidney injury, and arrhythmias, and identify Lichtenberg figures and cardiac arrest after lightning strike.
IN-10.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Toxins and environmental extremes: electrocution, lightning

IN-10.t: Explain how ionizing radiation damages DNA directly and through free radicals, and distinguish acute radiation dermatitis (erythema, desquamation) from chronic changes (atrophy, telangiectasia, fibrosis, obliterative endarteritis) and later skin cancers or angiosarcoma.
IN-10.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Toxins and environmental extremes: radiation

IN-10.t: Explain how sustained pressure and shear over bony prominences cause ischemic decubitus ulcers, stage them from nonblanching erythema to exposed bone, and explain how an auricular hematoma separating perichondrium from cartilage leads to cauliflower ear.
IN-10.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: ulcers, decubitus; cauliflower ear

IN-10.t: Explain how brown recluse spider venom (sphingomyelinase D) causes dermonecrosis with a central necrotic ulcer and, rarely, systemic hemolysis.
IN-10.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Venomous bites and stings: spider bites

IN-11.t: Explain how keratinocytes (Toll-like receptors, IL-1, TNF, defensins, cathelicidin), mast cells, and Langerhans cells provide innate defense, and trace Langerhans cell antigen capture and migration to regional lymph nodes to prime naive T cells.

Trace acute inflammation from vasodilation and venular leak (histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins) through rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins binding ICAM-1), transmigration (PECAM-1), and chemotaxis (C5a, LTB4, IL-8), and predict findings in leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.
IN-11.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders

IN-11.t: Explain how acute inflammation resolves, forms an abscess, or becomes chronic, and how Th1 cells and IFN-gamma activate macrophages to form granulomas, distinguishing caseating (tuberculosis) from noncaseating (sarcoidosis) granulomas.
IN-11.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders

IN-11.t: Classify skin reactions by hypersensitivity type: type I (urticaria, angioedema), type II (pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid), type III (Arthus reaction, leukocytoclastic vasculitis), and type IV (allergic contact dermatitis, tuberculin test), and predict the timing and mediators of each.
IN-11.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders

IN-11.t: Relate autoimmune skin findings to disease: malar and discoid lesions with interface dermatitis and junctional immune deposits in lupus, Gottron papules and heliotrope rash in dermatomyositis, and sclerodactyly with anticentromere or anti-Scl-70 antibodies in systemic sclerosis.
IN-11.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis; Musculoskeletal System: Inflammatory and immunologic disorders: dermatomyositis

IN-11.t: Explain how CD8 T cells and NK cells eliminate tumor cells, how tumors escape by losing MHC class I or expressing PD-L1, and why organ transplant recipients develop many cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas.

Explain how the recombinant HPV L1 virus-like particle vaccine induces neutralizing antibody, how live attenuated varicella vaccine induces both antibody and cell-mediated immunity, and why an Arthus (type III) local reaction can follow a toxoid booster.
IN-11.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Adverse effects of drugs: local reaction to vaccine

IN-12.t: Identify Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase and coagulase positive) and explain its virulence factors (protein A, Panton-Valentine leukocidin, exfoliative toxins, TSST-1) and how mecA-encoded PBP2a makes MRSA resistant to beta-lactams.
IN-12.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: MSSA and MRSA skin infections

IN-12.t: Identify Streptococcus pyogenes (beta-hemolytic, catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive), explain M protein, hyaluronic acid capsule, streptolysin O, streptokinase, and pyrogenic exotoxins, and explain why skin infection can cause glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever.
IN-12.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: erysipelas, impetigo, scarlet fever

IN-12.t: Explain how dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) use keratinases to live in stratum corneum, hair, and nails, identify septate hyphae on KOH prep, and contrast Malassezia (spaghetti and meatballs, hypopigmented or hyperpigmented tinea versicolor).
IN-12.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: fungal: dermatophytosis

IN-12.t: Identify Candida albicans as a dimorphic commensal forming budding yeast and pseudohyphae (germ tube positive), and explain how moisture, diabetes, antibiotics, glucocorticoids, and T cell or neutrophil defects allow mucocutaneous or invasive disease.
IN-12.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: fungal: candidiasis, skin

IN-12.t: Compare human papillomavirus (nonenveloped circular dsDNA, infects basal keratinocytes, koilocytes, E6 degrading p53 and E7 inactivating Rb in high-risk types) with molluscum contagiosum poxvirus (enveloped dsDNA replicating in cytoplasm, molluscum bodies) in structure, replication, and transmission.
IN-12.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: viral: molluscum contagiosum, verrucae vulgaris

IN-12.t: Explain how HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella zoster virus (enveloped dsDNA) infect epithelium, establish latency in sensory ganglia, and reactivate as herpes labialis, genital herpes, or dermatomal zoster, and identify multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear.
IN-12.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: viral: herpes simplex, herpes zoster

IN-12.t: Explain how Cutibacterium acnes (gram-positive anaerobic rod) lipases release free fatty acids and activate TLR2 in acne, and how Pseudomonas aeruginosa (gram-negative, oxidase positive) causes hot tub folliculitis.
IN-12.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: folliculitis; Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: acne vulgaris

IN-12.t: Identify vectors of skin-presenting infections: Ixodes ticks (Borrelia burgdorferi, erythema migrans), Dermacentor ticks (Rickettsia rickettsii, rash starting at wrists and ankles and spreading to the trunk, palms, and soles), sandflies (Leishmania), and dog and cat hookworm larvae in sand or soil (cutaneous larva migrans).
IN-12.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Infectious disorders: bacterial: Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever; Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: parasitic: cutaneous larva migrans, cutaneous leishmaniasis

IN-13-A.t: Explain how activating BRAF or NRAS mutations followed by oncogene-induced senescence produce nevocellular nevi, and classify junctional, compound, and intradermal nevi by nest location, relating this to patient age and to maturation of cells with depth.
IN-13-A.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: benign: pigmented nevi

IN-13-A.t: Distinguish a benign nevus (small, symmetric, uniform color, stable) from melanoma using ABCDE criteria, and identify large congenital melanocytic nevi as carrying increased melanoma risk.
IN-13-A.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: benign: pigmented nevi; Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Congenital disorders: congenital nevi

IN-13-A.t: Explain vitiligo as CD8 T cell destruction of melanocytes, identify sharply demarcated depigmented macules accentuated by Wood lamp, Koebner phenomenon, and absent melanocytes on biopsy, and relate it to autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes.
IN-13-A.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: autoimmune: vitiligo

IN-13-A.t: Distinguish vitiligo (melanocytes absent) from albinism (melanocytes present, melanin reduced), tinea versicolor, and postinflammatory hypopigmentation using distribution, Wood lamp, and KOH findings.
IN-13-A.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: autoimmune: vitiligo

IN-13-A.t: Distinguish ephelides (normal melanocyte number with more melanin, darken in sun) from lentigo simplex and solar lentigines (increased basal melanocytes) and from melasma linked to pregnancy and estrogen.
IN-13-A.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: disorders of pigmentation: lentigo

IN-13-A.t: Explain how high ACTH in primary adrenal insufficiency causes diffuse hyperpigmentation through POMC-derived MSH acting on melanocortin receptors, and why secondary adrenal insufficiency does not.
IN-13-A.usmle: Endocrine: Adrenal disorders: Corticoadrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)

IN-13-B.t: Explain atopic dermatitis as filaggrin-related barrier failure plus Th2 inflammation (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31 itch), and identify infant facial and extensor versus older flexural distribution, lichenification, the atopic triad, and Staphylococcus aureus and eczema herpeticum complications.
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: urticaria, erythema, exanthema: atopic dermatitis

IN-13-B.t: Distinguish allergic contact dermatitis (type IV, hapten sensitization via Langerhans cells, nickel or urushiol from poison ivy and oak, eruption 48 to 72 hours after re-exposure, positive patch test) from irritant contact dermatitis (direct damage, no sensitization).
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: papulosquamous and eczematous: contact dermatitis; dermatoses caused by plants

IN-13-B.t: Predict the distribution of contact dermatitis from the exposure (earlobes or wrist from nickel, linear vesicles from plants, hands from wet work) and identify spongiosis as its histologic hallmark.
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: papulosquamous and eczematous: contact dermatitis

IN-13-B.t: Explain erythema multiforme as a cytotoxic T cell reaction most often triggered by HSV (also Mycoplasma pneumoniae), and identify acral target lesions with dusky centers, limited mucosal involvement, and interface dermatitis with keratinocyte necrosis.
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: urticaria, erythema, exanthema: erythema multiforme

IN-13-B.t: Explain urticaria as mast cell degranulation (IgE-mediated, physical, or direct) causing superficial dermal edema with wheals lasting under 24 hours, and distinguish angioedema, chronic urticaria (over 6 weeks), and bradykinin-mediated C1 inhibitor deficiency without hives.
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: urticaria, erythema, exanthema: urticaria

IN-13-B.t: Distinguish Stevens-Johnson syndrome (under 10 percent body surface) from toxic epidermal necrolysis (over 30 percent) by extent of full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and identify mucosal involvement, positive Nikolsky sign, and drug triggers (sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol).
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: urticaria, erythema, exanthema: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis

IN-13-B.t: Identify pityriasis rosea by a herald patch followed by oval scaly patches along skin cleavage lines in a Christmas tree pattern on the trunk, resolving on its own within weeks.
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: urticaria, erythema, exanthema: pityriasis rosea

IN-13-B.t: Explain seborrheic dermatitis as an inflammatory response to Malassezia in sebaceous areas (scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds), identify greasy yellow scale and infant cradle cap, and relate severe disease to HIV and Parkinson disease.
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: hair and hair follicles: seborrheic dermatitis

IN-13-B.t: Identify recurrent aphthous ulcers as painful shallow ulcers with a yellow-gray base and red halo on nonkeratinized oral mucosa, and relate them to Behçet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and celiac disease.
IN-13-B.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: oral disease: aphthous ulcers

IN-13-C.t: Identify rosacea by central facial flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasias, and papules and pustules without comedones, identify triggers (heat, sunlight, alcohol, spicy food), and predict rhinophyma and ocular rosacea as complications.
IN-13-C.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: sweat and sebaceous glands: rosacea

IN-13-C.t: Distinguish rosacea from acne vulgaris (comedones, adolescents), seborrheic dermatitis (greasy scale), and the malar rash of lupus, which spares the nasolabial folds.
IN-13-C.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: sweat and sebaceous glands: rosacea

IN-13-C.t: Identify lichen planus by pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules with Wickham striae and reticular oral lesions, explain its band-like T cell infiltrate with sawtooth rete ridges and Civatte bodies, and relate it to hepatitis C.
IN-13-C.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: papulosquamous and eczematous: lichen planus

IN-13-C.t: Explain psoriasis as IL-23 and Th17 (IL-17) driven keratinocyte hyperproliferation with TNF and HLA-Cw6 risk, and identify silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces and scalp, Koebner phenomenon, nail pitting, and psoriatic arthritis.
IN-13-C.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: papulosquamous and eczematous: psoriasis

IN-13-C.t: Interpret psoriasis histology (acanthosis with regularly elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis, reduced stratum granulosum, thinned suprapapillary plates over dilated capillaries, Munro microabscesses) and relate the thin suprapapillary plates to the Auspitz sign.
IN-13-C.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: papulosquamous and eczematous: psoriasis

IN-13-C.t: Identify pyoderma gangrenosum as a neutrophilic dermatosis forming painful ulcers with violaceous undermined borders that worsen after trauma (pathergy), and relate it to inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and hematologic malignancy.
IN-13-C.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: vesiculobullous: pyoderma gangrenosum

IN-13-C.t: Explain hidradenitis suppurativa as chronic follicular occlusion in axillary, inguinal, and perineal skin that produces painful nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts, and scarring, and identify obesity and smoking as risk factors.
IN-13-C.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: sweat and sebaceous glands: hidradenitis suppurativa

IN-13-C.t: Distinguish nonscarring alopecias (alopecia areata from autoimmune attack on anagen follicles with exclamation point hairs, androgenetic alopecia from DHT-driven follicle miniaturization, telogen effluvium) from scarring alopecias that destroy follicles.
IN-13-C.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: hair and hair follicles: alopecia

IN-13-D.t: Compare the main types of epidermolysis bullosa by defective protein and split level: simplex (keratins 5 and 14, basal keratinocytes), junctional (laminin 332 or collagen XVII, lamina lucida), and dystrophic (type VII collagen, below the lamina densa).
IN-13-D.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: vesiculobullous: epidermolysis bullosa

IN-13-D.t: Predict the clinical course of epidermolysis bullosa, including blisters from minor friction beginning at birth, mucosal and nail involvement, and, in recessive dystrophic disease, scarring, fused digits, and aggressive squamous cell carcinoma.
IN-13-D.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: vesiculobullous: epidermolysis bullosa

IN-13-D.t: Explain bullous pemphigoid as IgG against hemidesmosomal BP180 and BP230 with complement and eosinophils, and identify tense subepidermal bullae in older adults, infrequent oral lesions, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane.
IN-13-D.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: vesiculobullous: pemphigoid

IN-13-D.t: Explain pemphigus vulgaris as IgG against desmoglein 3 (often also 1) causing suprabasal acantholysis with a tombstone basal layer, and identify flaccid bullae, early painful oral erosions, positive Nikolsky sign, and net-like intercellular IgG on immunofluorescence.
IN-13-D.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: vesiculobullous: pemphigus

IN-13-D.t: Distinguish pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus (desmoglein 1, subcorneal split, no mucosal lesions), and bullous pemphigoid by target antigen, split level, Nikolsky sign, mucosal involvement, and immunofluorescence pattern.
IN-13-D.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: vesiculobullous: pemphigus, pemphigoid

IN-13-D.t: Explain dermatitis herpetiformis as IgA against epidermal transglutaminase linked to celiac disease, and identify grouped pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces, neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillary tips, and granular IgA deposits.
IN-13-D.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: vesiculobullous: dermatitis herpetiformis

IN-13-E.t: Explain oculocutaneous albinism as autosomal recessive loss of tyrosinase or other melanosome proteins with normal melanocyte numbers, and predict photosensitivity, skin cancer risk, and visual problems such as nystagmus and reduced acuity.
IN-13-E.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: disorders of pigmentation: albinism

IN-13-E.t: Distinguish oculocutaneous albinism from X-linked ocular albinism and from the partial albinism of Chediak-Higashi syndrome (LYST defect, giant granules, recurrent pyogenic infections, neuropathy).
IN-13-E.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: disorders of pigmentation: albinism

IN-13-E.t: Explain how defects in collagen synthesis or processing cause Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, linking the classic type to type V collagen (COL5A1), the vascular type to type III collagen (COL3A1), and the kyphoscoliotic type to lysyl hydroxylase.
IN-13-E.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: structural protein disorders: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

IN-13-E.t: Identify skin features of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hyperextensible, soft, fragile skin, easy bruising, wide atrophic cigarette-paper scars) with joint hypermobility, and predict arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture and berry aneurysms in the vascular type.
IN-13-E.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: structural protein disorders: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

IN-13-E.t: Distinguish Ehlers-Danlos syndrome from Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1, tall stature, lens subluxation, aortic root dilation) and osteogenesis imperfecta (type I collagen, fractures, blue sclerae) by defective protein and findings.
IN-13-E.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: structural protein disorders

IN-13-F.t: Explain actinic keratosis as UV-induced keratinocyte dysplasia, identify rough sandpaper-like scaly papules on sun-exposed skin of older fair-skinned adults, lower epidermal atypia with parakeratosis and solar elastosis, and predict progression of some lesions to squamous cell carcinoma.
IN-13-F.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: benign: actinic keratoses

IN-13-F.t: Identify dysplastic nevi as larger than common nevi with irregular borders and variable pigment, with cytologic and architectural atypia on biopsy, and explain why multiple dysplastic nevi and familial CDKN2A mutation mark high melanoma risk.
IN-13-F.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: benign: pigmented nevi

IN-13-F.t: Identify seborrheic keratosis as a benign epidermal proliferation of older adults with a stuck-on waxy appearance, basaloid cells, horn cysts, and FGFR3 activating mutations, and interpret sudden eruption of many lesions as the Leser-Trélat sign.
IN-13-F.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: benign: seborrheic keratosis

IN-13-F.t: Relate mucocutaneous paraneoplastic signs to cancers: acanthosis nigricans and Leser-Trélat sign with gastric adenocarcinoma, dermatomyositis with ovarian, lung, and GI cancers, and paraneoplastic pemphigus with lymphoma, noting acanthosis nigricans more often reflects insulin resistance.
IN-13-F.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Neoplasms and related disorders: paraneoplastic syndromes: mucocutaneous

IN-13-F.t: Distinguish an epidermal inclusion cyst (stratified squamous lining with granular layer, laminated keratin, foreign body reaction on rupture) from a trichilemmal (pilar) cyst of the scalp, and identify lipoma as a soft, mobile, benign adipocyte tumor.
IN-13-F.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: benign: cysts, lipoma

IN-13-F.t: Distinguish infantile hemangioma (appears in the first weeks, proliferates, then involutes), cherry hemangioma of older adults, pyogenic granuloma (rapid, friable, bleeds, often in pregnancy), and port-wine stain (persistent capillary malformation, Sturge-Weber association).
IN-13-F.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: benign: hemangiomas

IN-13-F.t: Distinguish oral leukoplakia (white plaque that cannot be scraped off, linked to tobacco and alcohol, may show dysplasia and progress to squamous cell carcinoma) from oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV, lateral tongue, HIV) and thrush (scrapes off).
IN-13-F.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: oral disease: leukoplakia

IN-13-G.t: Explain basal cell carcinoma as the most common skin cancer, driven by UV and hedgehog activation, identify pearly papules with telangiectasias, rolled borders, or ulceration and basaloid nests with peripheral palisading, and predict local invasion with rare metastasis.
IN-13-G.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: malignant: basal cell carcinoma

IN-13-G.t: Identify risk factors for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cumulative UV, actinic keratosis, transplant immunosuppression, arsenic, HPV, xeroderma pigmentosum, chronic scars or ulcers giving Marjolin ulcer) and explain why it favors the lower lip and sun-exposed skin.
IN-13-G.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: malignant: squamous cell carcinoma

IN-13-G.t: Identify squamous cell carcinoma as a scaly, crusted, or ulcerated nodule with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, distinguish it from squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease) and keratoacanthoma, and predict higher metastatic risk than basal cell carcinoma.
IN-13-G.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: malignant: squamous cell carcinoma

IN-13-G.t: Explain melanoma risk factors (intense intermittent UV, fair skin, many or dysplastic nevi, family history, CDKN2A, xeroderma pigmentosum) and distinguish superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous, and mucosal (including genital) subtypes by site and behavior.
IN-13-G.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: malignant: melanoma, including genital

IN-13-G.t: Explain why entry into the vertical growth phase allows melanoma to metastasize, identify Breslow thickness as the key prognostic factor for localized melanoma, and identify S-100, HMB-45, and Melan-A as melanocytic immunostains.
IN-13-G.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: malignant: melanoma

IN-13-G.t: Describe mycosis fungoides as a cutaneous CD4 T cell lymphoma progressing through patch, plaque, and tumor stages with Pautrier microabscesses of cerebriform cells, and identify Sézary syndrome by erythroderma with circulating Sézary cells.
IN-13-G.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Neoplasms: malignant: cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, mycosis fungoides

IN-13-H.t: Explain the four steps of acne vulgaris (follicular hyperkeratinization, androgen-driven sebum, Cutibacterium acnes growth, inflammation), distinguish comedones from inflammatory papules, pustules, and nodules, and identify hyperandrogenism (polycystic ovary syndrome) and glucocorticoids as aggravating causes.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: sweat and sebaceous glands: acne vulgaris

IN-13-H.t: Identify cutaneous candidiasis by beefy red intertriginous plaques with satellite pustules, distinguish candidal diaper dermatitis (involves folds) from irritant diaper dermatitis (spares folds), and relate thrush and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis to host risk factors.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: fungal: candidiasis, skin; diaper rash

IN-13-H.t: Distinguish erysipelas (upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, raised sharply demarcated erythema, usually Streptococcus pyogenes) from cellulitis (deep dermis and subcutaneous fat, ill-defined borders, Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus) and relate each to its portal of entry.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: cellulitis, erysipelas

IN-13-H.t: Predict complications of cellulitis, including abscess, lymphangitis, bacteremia, and necrotizing fasciitis, suspected when pain is out of proportion to findings, with crepitus and rapid spread along fascial planes.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: cellulitis

IN-13-H.t: Explain erythema nodosum as a septal panniculitis without vasculitis, identify tender red nodules on the anterior shins that heal without scarring, and relate it to streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and pregnancy.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: urticaria, erythema, exanthema: erythema nodosum

IN-13-H.t: Distinguish folliculitis, furuncles, and carbuncles by depth and extent of follicular infection, mostly by Staphylococcus aureus, and identify hot tub folliculitis from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and cutaneous or pilonidal abscess as related suppurative lesions.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: folliculitis, carbuncle, abscess, pilonidal cyst

IN-13-H.t: Distinguish nonbullous impetigo (honey-colored crusts, Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes) from bullous impetigo (staphylococcal exfoliative toxin splitting the granular layer) in children, and predict poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis as a complication.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: impetigo

IN-13-H.t: Explain how MRSA carries mecA on SCCmec, distinguish community-acquired MRSA (Panton-Valentine leukocidin, recurrent abscesses and furuncles in athletes, crowded settings, and injection drug use) from hospital-acquired MRSA, and identify nasal colonization as a reservoir.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: MSSA and MRSA skin infections

IN-13-H.t: Identify molluscum contagiosum by firm, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication, spread by skin contact, autoinoculation, and sexual contact, with a self-limited course in children and extensive lesions in HIV.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: viral: molluscum contagiosum

IN-13-H.t: Classify tinea by site (capitis with kerion and alopecia, corporis with annular scaly border and central clearing, cruris, pedis, barbae, unguium or onychomycosis), and distinguish tinea versicolor as a Malassezia infection, not a dermatophytosis.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: fungal: dermatophytosis, tinea corporis, onychomycosis; Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Integumentary disorders: tinea barbae and capitis

IN-13-H.t: Distinguish common, plantar, flat, and anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum from HPV 6 and 11), identify papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and koilocytes on histology, and predict extensive warts with T cell immunodeficiency.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: viral: verrucae vulgaris

IN-13-H.t: Rank bloodborne pathogen transmission risk after a needle stick (hepatitis B highest, then hepatitis C, then HIV), and explain how a hollow-bore needle, deep injury, and high source viral load raise risk.

Predict the wound infection organism from context: Pasteurella multocida (cat or dog bite), Capnocytophaga canimorsus (dog bite with asplenia), Eikenella corrodens (human bite), Vibrio vulnificus and Mycobacterium marinum (water exposure), and Sporothrix schenckii (rose thorn).
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: animal bites

IN-13-H.t: Explain how Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin (lecithinase) causes gas gangrene with crepitus and myonecrosis, and how Clostridium tetani in a puncture wound releases tetanospasmin that blocks GABA and glycine release, causing spastic paralysis.
IN-13-H.usmle: Musculoskeletal System: Infectious disorders: clostridial myonecrosis (Clostridium perfringens); Nervous System: Infectious disorders: Clostridium tetani

IN-13-H.t: Identify herpes simplex skin infections (herpes labialis, genital herpes, herpetic whitlow, eczema herpeticum) and herpes zoster (painful dermatomal vesicles, Ramsay Hunt syndrome with facial palsy and ear vesicles), and predict postherpetic neuralgia.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: viral: herpes simplex, herpes zoster, Ramsay-Hunt syndrome

IN-13-H.t: Distinguish viral exanthems: measles (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, rash spreading down from the head), rubella (postauricular nodes, milder rash), roseola (HHV-6, high fever then rash), and erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19, slapped cheek, lacy rash).
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: viral: measles, rubella, roseola, erythema infectiosum

IN-13-H.t: Distinguish varicella (crops of vesicles in different stages starting on the trunk), hand-foot-and-mouth disease and herpangina (coxsackievirus A), and scarlet fever (sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor, desquamation from streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin).
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: viral: chickenpox, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, herpangina; bacterial: scarlet fever

IN-13-H.t: Distinguish staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (young children, toxin cleaves desmoglein 1 in the granular layer, mucosa spared) from toxic epidermal necrolysis (drug-triggered full-thickness epidermal necrosis with mucosal involvement) by split level and cause.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome

IN-13-H.t: Compare tuberculoid leprosy (Th1, few bacilli, few hypopigmented anesthetic plaques) with lepromatous leprosy (Th2, many bacilli, diffuse nodules, leonine facies), and explain why Mycobacterium leprae favors cool skin and peripheral nerves and cannot be cultured in vitro.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: mycobacterial infections, leprosy

IN-13-H.t: Explain how Bacillus anthracis edema factor (adenylate cyclase), lethal factor, protective antigen, and polypeptide capsule produce cutaneous anthrax, a painless papule that becomes a black eschar surrounded by edema.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: bacterial: anthrax

IN-13-H.t: Identify scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei burrows in web spaces, wrists, and genitals, nocturnal itch, crusted scabies with immunosuppression), head and pubic lice, body lice as vectors of Rickettsia prowazekii and Bartonella quintana, and bedbug bites in linear clusters.
IN-13-H.usmle: Skin & Subcutaneous Tissue: Infectious disorders: infestations: scabies, lice, insect bites
